title: Dhul Qa'dah

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eid al-Fitr: dates before the prayer, and a different road back. Your line was a new road home. Which road did you take, and who was on it? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-three.

A suitcase lies open on a bed, half full. Two lengths of plain white cloth, folded. A small bottle of unscented soap. A list on the fridge of people to call before leaving: an aunt, an old friend, a neighbor they once argued with. Someone in the house is going on hajj, and the house knows it. The calendar has turned to Dhul Qa'dah, one of the sacred months from earlier on the path. Nothing big happens in it on the calendar. But in houses like this one, bags are being packed. Today, the month of getting ready to go.
screen: `A SUITCASE, HALF FULL.` → `PEOPLE TO CALL BEFORE LEAVING.` → `THE MONTH OF GETTING READY.`

segments.voice: Four things about this quiet month. First, it sits inside the season of the pilgrimage. The Qur'an says, in Surah al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's translation: "The pilgrimage is (in) the well-known months." Tradition counts Dhul Qa'dah among those months, so travelers can already be on the road. Second, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, chose this month for his own journeys to Makkah. Anas reports in al-Bukhari that the Prophet's 'umrahs, the lesser pilgrimages, were in Dhul Qa'dah, except the one he joined to his hajj. So the month already has footsteps in it. Third, packing. The same verse goes on: "So make provision for yourselves (Hereafter); for the best provision is to ward off evil." Pack your bag, it says, and then names a provision no bag can hold. So for some pilgrims, getting ready isn't only tickets and white cloth. It's paying back what they owe, asking forgiveness from people they've wronged, making the calls on the fridge list. Fourth, the people who stay. A traveler is sent off with words. In al-Tirmidhi, there's a report that when someone was leaving, the Prophet would say, in paraphrase: I entrust to Allah your religion, what you've been trusted with, and the last of your deeds. Not a wish for good weather. A handing over. The pilgrims set out, and the ones at home hand them over.
screen: `THE WELL-KNOWN MONTHS.` · `THE PROPHET'S 'UMRAHS.` · `THE BEST PROVISION.` · `HANDING THE TRAVELER OVER.`

segments.voice: The practice: keep the pilgrims in mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who is going, or has gone, or someday hopes to go. If no one comes, picture a stranger at an airport gate in white, a little nervous, holding a passport. Stay with them for a few breaths. Their packing. Their goodbyes. The road ahead. If you pray, you can pray for the pilgrims in your own words, or use the Prophet's farewell: I entrust you to Allah. If you don't, simply wish them a safe road and a good return. The bell holds the time.
Dhul Qa'dah. A sacred month, the month before the hajj, when the Prophet made his 'umrahs and when pilgrims pack, settle their debts and say their goodbyes. Today's word.

Your line: the pilgrims set out. Today, settle one small thing you'd want settled before a long trip: a message, a debt, an apology. Tomorrow, Dhul Hijjah at home. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: In Dhul Qa'dah, Muslims preparing for hajj often settle debts, ask forgiveness of family and friends, and gather their simple white garments, and families and mosques send them off with prayers for a safe journey.

fork.setup: you're packing for the pilgrimage. the verse says make provision for yourselves. what does it call the best provision?
fork.reveal: "for the best provision is to ward off evil." the verse starts with packing and ends with something no bag can hold.

original.note: Arabic: the name of a sacred month, the first of the three that come one after another.

trapdoor: what you thought: a quiet month with nothing in it.
what it means: the month of getting ready: packing, debts settled, goodbyes said, pilgrims sent off.
what a scholar hears: al-Baqarah 2:197 on the well-known months and the best provision, and Anas in al-Bukhari placing the Prophet's 'umrahs in Dhul Qa'dah.

notes: Verify Pickthall's exact wording of 2:197, including the parentheses '(in)' and '(Hereafter)'.
'Dhul Qa'dah is among the months the scholars count in that season': the well-known months are usually given as Shawwal, Dhul Qa'dah and (part of) Dhul Hijjah; confirm the phrasing.
The original note calls Dhul Qa'dah the first of the three sacred months in a row, following day 1353's teaching from Bukhari (Abu Bakrah); confirm.
Confirm Bukhari 1778 and Tirmidhi 3443 numbering and the paraphrase of the farewell.
Settling debts and asking forgiveness before hajj are described as what some pilgrims do; confirm.
